title: Simson's Line Theorem
description: Simson's theorem as a biconditional: the feet of the perpendiculars from a point P to the three side-lines of triangle ABC are collinear if and only if P lies on the circumcircle of ABC. Formalized in complex coordinates with the circumcircle normalised to the unit circle.

originalContributions: FeetCollinear a b c p: the pedal-triangle collinearity criterion (F_BC − F_AB)·conj(F_CA − F_AB) = conj(F_BC − F_AB)·(F_CA − F_AB) packaged as a reusable predicate over an arbitrary point P (no unit-circle assumption on P)

simson_defect: the sharp collinearity-defect identity (F_BC − F_AB)·conj(F_CA − F_AB) − conj(F_BC − F_AB)·(F_CA − F_AB) = (a−c)(c−b)(a−b)/(4abc)·(1 − p·conj p), the off-circle generalisation of the base file's simson_key, proved by foot_diff/foot_diff' + conj z = z⁻¹ + field_simp + ring

feet_collinear_iff: the full biconditional — for a nondegenerate triangle on the unit circle, the three pedal feet are collinear if and only if Complex.normSq p = 1 (P on the circumcircle); the nonzero triangle prefactor is factored out so vanishing of the defect is equivalent to 1 − |P|² = 0

Four self-contained unit-circle helper lemmas (ne_zero_of_normSq_one, conj_eq_inv, im_eq_zero_of_conj_eq, conj_eq_of_im_eq_zero) supplying the conj z = z⁻¹ substitution and the real-axis bridges used throughout; entire development axiom-free and sorry-free

sections.title: Unit-Circle Helper Lemmas
sections.description: Four private lemmas about a point on the unit circle: ne_zero_of_normSq_one (normSq z = 1 ⟹ z ≠ 0), conj_eq_inv (conj z = z⁻¹ on the circle), and the two real-axis bridges im_eq_zero_of_conj_eq (conj z = z ⟹ z.im = 0) and conj_eq_of_im_eq_zero (z.im = 0 ⟹ conj z = z).

sections.title: The Collinearity Predicate
sections.description: def FeetCollinear a b c p: the complex criterion (F_BC − F_AB)·conj(F_CA − F_AB) = conj(F_BC − F_AB)·(F_CA − F_AB) that the pedal-triangle cross product is real — the conclusion of SimsonLineTheorem.simson_key, packaged as a reusable predicate.

sections.title: The Collinearity-Defect Identity
sections.description: theorem simson_defect: with a, b, c on the unit circle but P free, the collinearity defect of the three pedal feet collapses to (a−c)(c−b)(a−b)/(4abc)·(1 − p·conj p). Proved by rewriting with the base file's foot_diff/foot_diff', substituting conj z = z⁻¹, then field_simp and ring. This off-circle generalisation of simson_key is the crux of the converse.

sections.title: The Biconditional
sections.description: theorem feet_collinear_iff: for a nondegenerate triangle (a ≠ b, b ≠ c, c ≠ a) on the unit circle, the pedal feet are collinear ⟺ Complex.normSq p = 1. The nonzero triangle prefactor is factored out (hK), so the defect vanishes iff 1 − p·conj p = 0; both directions are read off via mul_eq_zero and mul_conj.

overview.historicalContext:
The Simson line is named after the Scottish mathematician Robert Simson (1687–1768), though the result does not appear in his surviving work; it was first explicitly published by William Wallace in 1797 and is sometimes called the Wallace line. The theorem is a cornerstone of triangle geometry: it characterizes the circumcircle as exactly the locus of points whose three perpendicular feet onto the side-lines are collinear (a point off the circumcircle produces a genuine 'pedal triangle' of positive area).

The Simson line carries a rich further structure. As P traverses the circumcircle, the Simson line envelopes a deltoid (Steiner's deltoid), and the Simson lines of diametrically opposite points are perpendicular. The Simson line of P also bisects the segment joining P to the orthocenter of the triangle. These refinements make the Simson line a gateway to the deeper projective and metric geometry of the triangle.

The complex-number proof used here is the standard modern treatment: placing the circumcircle at the unit circle turns the orthogonal projection onto a chord into a rational expression in the vertices and their conjugates, and the unit-circle constraint conj z = 1/z collapses the collinearity condition to a polynomial identity.
overview.problemStatement: **Simson's Line Theorem**: Let ABC be a triangle and P a point on its circumcircle. Let F_AB, F_BC, F_CA be the feet of the perpendiculars dropped from P onto the lines AB, BC, CA respectively. Then F_AB, F_BC, F_CA are collinear; the line through them is called the Simson line (or Wallace line) of P with respect to the triangle.
overview.text: For a point P on the circumcircle of a triangle, the three feet of the perpendiculars from P to the sides of the triangle lie on a single line — the Simson line.
overview.proofStrategy:
The proof uses **complex coordinates** with the circumcircle normalised to the **unit circle**.

1. **Foot formula**: For u, v on the unit circle, the foot of the perpendicular from any p onto the chord-line uv has the closed form foot(u,v,p) = (u + v + p − u·v·conj p)/2. This is verified to be the orthogonal projection by checking perpendicularity (Re((p−foot)·conj(v−u)) = 0) and incidence on the line (Im((foot−u)·conj(v−u)) = 0).

2. **Difference identity**: foot(b,c,p) − foot(a,b,p) = (c−a)(1 − b·conj p)/2, a pure algebraic identity. Symmetrically, foot(c,a,p) − foot(a,b,p) = (c−b)(1 − a·conj p)/2.

3. **Collinearity criterion**: three complex points are collinear iff w = (z₂−z₁)·conj(z₃−z₁) is real, i.e. w = conj w (equivalently Im w = 0, the vanishing of the signed area). Applying this to the three feet and substituting conj z = z⁻¹ (valid on the unit circle) reduces the statement to a rational-function identity, closed by field_simp and ring.

4. **Converse (biconditional)**: this file keeps conj p free, turning the defect computation into the identity (F_BC − F_AB)·conj(F_CA − F_AB) − conj(…)·(…) = (a−c)(c−b)(a−b)/(4abc)·(1 − p·conj p) (simson_defect). For distinct vertices the prefactor is nonzero, so collinearity of the feet forces 1 − |P|² = 0, i.e. P lies on the circumcircle. This gives the headline biconditional feet_collinear_iff, with the forward direction recovered as its mpr half (simson_forward) and a signed-area restatement (feet_collinear_iff_signed_area).
keyInsights: **Unit-circle normalisation**: placing the circumcircle at |z| = 1 makes conj z = z⁻¹, turning conjugation into a rational operation and the whole theorem into a polynomial identity
**Closed-form foot**: foot(u,v,p) = (u+v+p − u·v·conj p)/2 packages the orthogonal projection onto a chord; it needs only u, v on the circle, not p
**Difference identity**: foot(b,c,p) − foot(a,b,p) = (c−a)(1 − b·conj p)/2 is a pure ring fact — the geometric content is entirely in this factorisation through the chord direction c−a
**Real-ratio = collinear**: the classical criterion that (z₂−z₁)·conj(z₃−z₁) ∈ ℝ encodes collinearity (its imaginary part is twice the signed area of the triangle of feet)
**Circumcircle is essential**: the same computation off the unit circle yields a nonzero signed area, recovering the converse that only circumcircle points give a degenerate pedal triangle

**Free conj p ⇒ biconditional**: not assuming P on the circle yields the defect identity (a-c)(c-b)(a-b)/(4abc)·(1 - p·conj p) (simson_defect); the factor 1 - |P|² makes collinearity of the feet equivalent to P being on the circumcircle, giving the full iff (feet_collinear_iff)
prerequisites: Complex numbers and arithmetic in ℂ
The unit-circle identity conj z = z⁻¹
Collinearity of complex points via the vanishing imaginary part of a cross product
openQuestions: Can the Steiner deltoid (the envelope of all Simson lines as P moves on the circumcircle) be formalized? This needs a tangency/envelope argument rather than the pure-ring engine used here.

The defect identity simson_defect measures how far the pedal feet are from collinear when P is off the circumcircle; can this quantitative defect be related to the distance from P to the circle, or to the area of the pedal triangle, in closed form?

The imported base development already formalizes the bisection of segment PH and the nine-point-circle membership of that bisection point; can the full nine-point circle (all nine classical points) be characterized in the same complex-coordinate framework?

conclusion.summary: Building on the imported base development (which proves the forward direction via the closed-form perpendicular foot foot(u,v,p) = (u+v+p − u·v·conj p)/2), this file closes the converse and completes Simson's theorem to a full biconditional. Keeping conj p free yields the collinearity-defect identity simson_defect = (a−c)(c−b)(a−b)/(4abc)·(1 − p·conj p), whose 1 − |P|² factor delivers both directions: for a nondegenerate triangle on the unit circle the pedal feet are collinear iff P lies on the circumcircle (feet_collinear_iff), with the forward half recovered as simson_forward and a signed-area restatement in feet_collinear_iff_signed_area. All steps are discharged by the conj z = z⁻¹ substitution with field_simp and ring; no axioms, no sorries.
conclusion.implications: **Theoretical Significance**: The proof again demonstrates the leverage of complex coordinates in classical plane geometry: a metric statement about perpendicular feet on a circle becomes a rational identity. The unit-circle substitution conj z = z⁻¹ is the same device that powers the complex proofs of Ptolemy's and Napoleon's theorems, situating Simson's line within a common algebraic toolkit for circle and triangle geometry. Isolating the converse as a single defect identity valid for an arbitrary P shows that the circumcircle is not merely sufficient but necessary for collinearity of the pedal feet.
openQuestions: Can the Steiner deltoid envelope of Simson lines be formalized (needs a tangency/envelope argument)?
Can the quantitative collinearity defect (nonzero when P is off the circumcircle) be expressed in closed form in terms of the distance from P to the circle?

The base development already formalizes the Simson-line/orthocenter bisection and the nine-point-circle membership of the bisection point; can the complete nine-point circle be characterized in this framework?

crossReferences.description: Both reduce a classical triangle theorem to a complex-coordinate identity; Napoleon uses a rotation identity while Simson uses the unit-circle substitution conj z = z⁻¹ for perpendicular feet
Both are circle theorems proved by the same complex device: normalising to the unit circle so that conj z = 1/z turns the geometric condition into an algebraic identity
